item.passage:
Pepper, the hamster who lived in a glass tank in Mr. Tan's sixth-grade science room, went home with Jonah Price for winter break because Jonah's name was the only one on the sign-up sheet. His mother had agreed on two conditions: the tank stayed in his room, and she would hear nothing about it for ten days.

For three days she heard nothing. Jonah changed the bedding, refilled the water bottle, and wrote in the notebook Mr. Tan had sent along, which asked for the date, the food given, and "anything unusual." Under "anything unusual" he wrote "ran on wheel 2 hrs" and then, the next night, "ran on wheel 3 hrs."

On the fourth morning the screen lid of the tank was pushed up at one corner, and the tank was empty.

Jonah stood very still in the middle of his room and listened. He heard the furnace, and a car door outside, and his mother downstairs talking back to the radio. He heard no hamster.

He closed his door and searched the room: under the bed, behind the bookcase, inside each of his shoes. Then he sat down on the floor and thought about what Pepper wanted. Food, mostly. In the notebook he had written that Pepper ate her sunflower seeds first and left the pellets for later.

From the kitchen cupboard he took the bag of sunflower seeds his mother put out for the birds. He went through the house, upstairs and down, and in each room he set exactly ten seeds in a little pile against the wall: his room, his parents' room, the bathroom, the hall closet, the kitchen, the living room, the laundry room. He wrote the rooms in the notebook, with a 10 beside each one. Under "anything unusual" for the fourth day he wrote only "lid open."

His mother asked at supper why there were birdseeds in the hall closet. Jonah said it was an experiment, which was true.

In the morning he checked every pile. Six piles still had ten seeds. The pile in the laundry room had three. Behind the dryer, wedged in a nest of lint and one of his father's socks, Pepper was asleep with her cheeks full.

Jonah carried her upstairs in both hands. He pressed the corner of the lid down, set a dictionary on top of it, and opened the notebook. Under "anything unusual" for the fifth day he wrote: "Found her. Laundry room. 7 seeds."

When school started again, Mr. Tan read the notebook at his desk while Jonah waited. He turned the page, read the fifth day twice, and leaned forward.

"Seven seeds," he said. "How did you know it was seven?"

Jonah turned back one page, to the list of rooms with a 10 beside each, and held it out to him.

All winter it talks to itself in the corner,
a row of iron ribs under the window
painted so many times the paint has a paint.
At six it begins: a knock, a long hiss,

then the clanking, like someone in the cellar
dropping a wrench and picking it up and dropping it,
and my grandmother, who has lived here forty years,
says that is the heat climbing the stairs.

I lay my mittens across it to dry.
My brother sets his boots near enough to steam.
The cat has claimed the top, a narrow shelf
too hot for a hand, which she endures

the way a queen endures a hard throne.
Our landlord says it is older than the building's
elevator, older than the stoplight on the corner,
that it came up from the cellar in pieces

and was fitted together here, rib by rib,
by men who are all gone now. Some nights
the hissing sounds almost like words,
some phrase it has been trying for years to finish.

My grandmother says it is only steam.
She says it the way she says a lot of things,
to keep us from thinking too much, and then
she holds her hands out to it, palms flat,

like a person warming herself at a fire
she has known since before we were born,
which she has. In the morning the frost
on the glass above it has a clear round hole.

item.passage:
I was twelve before anyone found out that I needed glasses, which means that for several years I lived in a world where trees were green clouds on brown sticks. I thought everyone saw them that way. I thought the word leaves was something people said about trees in general, the way they said forest about a lot of trees, and that only up close, holding one in your hand, did a leaf become a separate thing.

It came out during a school eye screening in the gym. The nurse pointed at the chart on the far wall and asked me to read the third line, and I asked her which wall she meant. She wrote something on her form and gave me a folded note for my parents, which I read on the bus. It said that I should see an eye doctor "at your earliest convenience," and it had the word urgent written in pencil at the top and then erased.

My mother took me to an optometrist in a strip mall between a laundromat and a dentist. He put a heavy black machine in front of my face and flipped lenses into place, one after another, asking "Better here, or here?" For most of the questions I could not tell the difference. Then, partway through, he flipped a lens in and the chart on the wall went sharp, every letter at once, and I laughed out loud.

The glasses took a week. I picked them up on a Saturday morning, and when we walked out of the store I stopped on the sidewalk and stood there long enough that my mother came back for me. Across the parking lot was a row of maple trees, and every tree was made of leaves. Thousands of them, each one a separate shape, each one moving a little on its own in the wind. I had walked past those trees my whole life.

I remember feeling two things at once. The first was simple delight, the kind you feel when a magician turns a handkerchief into a dove. The second took me longer to name. It was something like embarrassment on behalf of my younger self, who had been so sure the world was blurry at the edges that it never occurred to her to ask.

I have worn glasses for thirty years now, and I still take them off sometimes, on a walk, to look at a row of trees the old way. It is a kind of reminder. What I saw at twelve was the world as it had always been. What changed was only that I could finally see it.

I was twelve before anyone found out that I needed glasses, which means that for several years I lived in a world where trees were green clouds on brown sticks. I thought everyone saw them that way. I thought the word leaves was something people said about trees in general, the way they said forest about a lot of trees, and that only up close, holding one in your hand, did a leaf become a separate thing.

It came out during a school eye screening in the gym. The nurse pointed at the chart on the far wall and asked me to read the third line, and I asked her which wall she meant. She wrote something on her form and gave me a folded note for my parents, which I read on the bus. It said that I should see an eye doctor "at your earliest convenience," and it had the word urgent written in pencil at the top and then erased.

My mother took me to an optometrist in a strip mall between a laundromat and a dentist. He put a heavy black machine in front of my face and flipped lenses into place, one after another, asking "Better here, or here?" For most of the questions I could not tell the difference. Then, partway through, he flipped a lens in and the chart on the wall went sharp, every letter at once, and I laughed out loud.

The glasses took a week. I picked them up on a Saturday morning, and when we walked out of the store I stopped on the sidewalk and stood there long enough that my mother came back for me. Across the parking lot was a row of maple trees, and every tree was made of leaves. Thousands of them, each one a separate shape, each one moving a little on its own in the wind. I had walked past those trees my whole life.

I remember feeling two things at once. The first was simple delight, the kind you feel when a magician turns a handkerchief into a dove. The second took me longer to name. It was something like embarrassment on behalf of my younger self, who had been so sure the world was blurry at the edges that it never occurred to her to ask.

I have worn glasses for thirty years now, and I still take them off sometimes, on a walk, to look at a row of trees the old way. It is a kind of reminder. What I saw at twelve was the world as it had always been. What changed was only that I could finally see it.

item.passage:
Two years ago my husband and I made a rule that each of our children, starting at thirteen, would cook dinner for the family one night a week. The rule had exactly three parts. The cook chooses the meal. The cook shops for it, within a budget we agree on. And the rest of us eat what is served, without comment, for the first three months.

Friends assumed we had done this to get a night off, and I will admit that was part of it. But the reason we have kept it going is that cooking a full meal teaches something that very little else in a teenager's week does: how to make several things come out right at the same moment.

Anyone can follow a recipe. Following three at once is a different skill. The rice needs twenty minutes, the chicken needs thirty, and the salad needs five but will wilt if it sits, so the cook has to work backward from the moment the food reaches the table. Our son, Theo, served his first dinner in three courses he had not intended: rice at six, chicken at six-thirty, and salad, which he had forgotten, at a quarter to seven. By his fourth week the plates arrived together.

The budget turned out to matter more than I expected. Our daughter, June, discovered in her first month that the recipe she had chosen called for pine nuts, and that pine nuts cost about as much per pound as a good steak. She stood in the grocery aisle doing arithmetic on her phone and came home with sunflower seeds instead. When the three months of silence were over, the first thing we told her was that we had preferred the sunflower seeds.

The third rule, eating without comment, was the hardest one for the adults. It is very tempting to tell a thirteen-year-old that the pasta is gummy. But a cook who expects to be graded every night learns to make only the safe things, and we wanted our children to try the hard ones. So for three months we ate gummy pasta, and pale chicken, and one memorable soup, and said thank you. Our silence was the price of their nerve.

Our children are unlikely to become professional cooks, and that was never the point. The point is that somewhere in the middle of a Tuesday evening, with a pot about to boil over and the bread still in the oven, each of them has learned to look up from the cutting board and think about what has to happen next.

In the summer of 1888 the railroad depot at Pruett's Crossing began receiving a weather forecast by telegraph every morning. The forecast came from the national weather office, which collected reports from stations across the country, drew them on a map, and sent its predictions down the wires to towns along the railroad lines.

The depot agent, Samuel Orr, was expected to make the forecast public. For this the government had sent him a set of cotton flags and a printed card explaining them. A white flag meant fair weather. A blue flag meant rain or snow. A black triangle flown above either one meant warmer weather was coming, and flown below it, colder. Orr ran the flags up a pole on the roof of the grain elevator, the tallest building for miles, where farmers could see them from their fields.

At first the flags were mostly a joke. Men at the feed store called them the government's washing and asked Orr whether he had hung out his shirts to dry. A farmer named Elias Booker said he had his own forecast, which was his left knee, and that it had never once needed a telegraph.

Orr was a careful man, and the jokes bothered him less than the fact that he had no way to answer them. In September he began keeping a ledger. Each morning he wrote down the flags he had raised, and each evening he wrote down the weather that had actually come. At the end of every week he copied the totals onto a sheet of paper and pinned it in the depot window: so many days right, so many wrong.

The sheet was read far more closely than the flags had ever been. Farmers stopped to check it when they brought grain to the elevator. By the end of the first year the forecasts had been right on roughly three days in four, and the men at the feed store had begun to argue about the numbers instead of the flags. Booker came in one October afternoon and asked to see the ledger itself. He went down the columns with his finger for a long time.

The following summer, when a blue flag went up on a clear July morning, Booker left his hay standing in the field. It rained that afternoon. He told the men at the feed store that his knee had said the same thing, though he admitted it had said so rather more quietly.

A seed that travels even a short distance away has a better chance of finding an open patch of sunlight.

The maple's answer is the samara, the winged fruit that children call a helicopter. Each samara holds a single seed at one end, heavy and round, and a thin, papery wing at the other. On many maples the samaras grow in joined pairs, which split apart before or as they fall.

Drop a samara from a balcony and it does not simply flutter down. Within a fraction of a second it begins to spin, the heavy seed at the center of the turn and the wing sweeping around it like the blade of a slow propeller. The spinning sharply slows its fall. A samara that would drop like a pebble without its wing may take several times as long to reach the ground, and every extra second in the air is a second in which the wind can push it sideways.

For many years scientists were puzzled by how much lift such a small, simple wing could produce. In 2009 a team of researchers filmed falling maple seeds and found part of the answer. As the wing spins, a small whirl of air forms along its leading edge and stays attached there, lowering the air pressure above the wing and adding lift. Some insects, and hovering birds such as hummingbirds, keep a similar whirl of air on their wings.

Even with this help, most samaras land close to home. On a calm day the great majority come down within a few dozen meters of the tree. But on a windy day some are carried much farther, and a tree that drops many thousands of seeds a year needs only a handful to land in good places. Spinning does not guarantee that any one seed will succeed. It shifts the odds, a little, for each of them.
